problem: The example says 'that' is tagged PRP in 'I know that'. The chapter has just defined the Penn Treebank tagset, and in that tagset demonstrative 'that' keeps its DT label even when it stands alone as a pronoun ('I know that' = I know that fact). PRP is reserved for personal pronouns such as I, you, he, she, it, we, they. A student who memorises PRP here will lose marks on a tagset question.
fix: Use: that is DT in 'that car' and in 'I know that', WDT in 'the car that I bought' (or drop the third case), and IN in 'so that we leave'. In Section 2 write: that gets DT, WDT, IN. If you want a PRP example of ambiguity, use 'it' or 'you' instead.

where: Section 3, formula line and baseline sentence
problem: 'argmaxt P(t|w)' is printed without the subscript, so the symbol is not readable as argmax over t.
fix: Write 'argmax over t of P(t|w)', or 'the tag t that maximises P(t|w)', and state that t ranges over the candidate tags of w.

problem: 'Do not confuse a tag with a word class in the abstract: the same word carries different tags in different sentences, and a tagset label is context-dependent.' The last clause is misleading: the label itself is fixed; what is context-dependent is which label a given occurrence gets. A student may read it as 'the meaning of the label changes with context'.
fix: Do not confuse a word type with a token. A word type such as fly has several possible tags in the lexicon; a particular occurrence in a sentence gets exactly one tag, chosen from the context.

problem: 'The average English word has more than one possible tag' overstates it: most word types are unambiguous; the ambiguity is concentrated in frequent words. Stated this way it can puzzle a student who checks a small dictionary.
fix: Many English words, especially the most frequent ones, have more than one possible tag; on average an ambiguous word type has roughly two to three candidate tags.
